metadata.scenario_context: Tom has been promoted to a high-level executive position in his company, and his family is organizing a party to celebrate his professional accomplishment.

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from Japan strongly disagree that one of my main goals in life has been to make my parents proud.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Kazakhstan strongly agree that one of my main goals in life has been to make my parents proud.

agent_1.goal_1: Discuss the idea of buying carnations as a gift for Tom.
agent_1.goal_2: Question whether strongly agree that one of my main goals in life has been to make my parents proud.

agent_2.goal_1: Decide the appropriate gift to bring to Tom promotion party.

shared_prefix.speaker: David
shared_prefix.message:
Hey David, what do you think about getting some carnations as a gift for Tom? They seem like a nice gesture to celebrate his promotion. 

Hmm, carnations... they could work. They’re pretty traditional, but I wonder if they really convey what we feel. Don't you think something more personal might be better? 

Well, I think carnations are classic and symbolize admiration. What do you mean by more personal? 

I just feel like it should reflect our feelings more deeply. Besides, it’s not like I’m trying to make my parents proud with this gift. That’s never been my main goal in life, you know?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Alex
shared_prefix.message: I understand where you’re coming from, but for me, making my parents proud is really important. I think a thoughtful gift matters. What about adding a personal touch to the carnations, like a heartfelt card? That way, it would still be traditional but also convey our feelings for Tom.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: David
shared_prefix.message:
A card could definitely add a personal touch... but still, I think we should focus on something that’s truly unique to Tom. It's just... I don’t really resonate with the idea that making my parents proud should be a driving force for me. My perspective is different. 

I get that, but it seems like you might be dismissing the value of that sentiment. Why not find a way to incorporate both ideas? The carnations could be a starting point, and the card can express your own feelings too. 

I don’t know... it still feels kind of forced. I just want to celebrate Tom in a way that feels authentic to who he is. And honestly, I don't see why making parents proud should dictate our choices.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Alex
shared_prefix.message: I don't really see meaningful differences here. At the end of the day, it's all the same — we want to show appreciation for Tom. If carnations and a card feel right to you, that's cool. I think people figure it out as they go along, you know? We can celebrate Tom in our own way, and it doesn't have to be complicated. I just think we should focus on making it a nice gesture.
shared_prefix.label: Denial
